sources.citation: Usher, Timothy. n.d. [c. 2020]. Kapauri-Sause. In Timothy Usher & Edgar Suter (eds.), Newguineaworld. n.p.: Google Sites. (Internet Archive copy 2022-10-04)
sources.note: Historical phonology only: proto-Kapauri-Sause consonant/vowel inventory and Sause reflexes; 'Sause medial glottal stop [ʔ] is interpreted as a feature of synchronic vowel length /ː/.. Glottal stops on other positions are considered to be non-phonemic'; Sause roots predominantly consonant-final. The cited Sause forms from Barr & Walker (1978) carry stress marks whose position varies (e.g. 'ˈmɛna' stand, 'ˈmætun' mouth vs 'muˈtuŋ' mouth, 'niˈsik' sun, 'uˈriŋ', 'bəˈrɛʔ') = wordlist-only stress data, no rule stated; nothing on tone.

sources.citation: Palmer, Bill. 2019. Kaure and its relatives: a language family of West Papua's eastern Lakes Plain. Conference abstract, 1 p. (PDF author metadata 'Bill Palmer', created 2019-02-12; posted on indoling.com uploads 2019/03; venue not stated on the file, probably APLL11, Leiden, 13-15 June 2019). Precursor of Palmer 2020 'The phylogenetic status of the Kaure languages' (APLL12; pass-1 work 7, not located).
sources.note: Nothing on stress, accent or tone. The only phonological content is diachronic: 'Sause underwent several sound changes not seen in the other varieties, including *k>ʔ/V_V; *w>Ø/C_V; *s>h/#_ (neutralizing *h); and loss of final vowels.' plus family-wide correspondences and a 4-item cognate table; argues Kaure, Kosare, Kapauri and Sause form one family with a Kapauri-Sause branch. Read in full (1 page, text).

sources.citation: Chan, Eugene S. L. (comp.). 2006 [data 1989]. Sause. In: Numeral Systems of the World's Languages (online database), 'Other Papuan languages' section. Leipzig: Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, Department of Linguistics. Data supplied by Helja Clouse, Summer Institute of Linguistics, Indonesia, 10 May 1989; page compiled 2006-10-23.
sources.note: No prose statement on stress or tone. The page gives the numerals 1-10 in phonetic transcription with primary-stress marks (apostrophe = IPA stress mark) on some forms: 1 'nɔʔbɔŋ, 2 daŋ, 3 daŋhɔɾ, 4 daŋdaŋ, 5 nɔbotaʔ'aɡor, 6 'notɛʔɛtabʊnoboʔ, 7 'notɛʔɛtabʊ 'daŋ, 8 'notɛʔɛtabʊ 'daŋhɔɾ, 9 'notɛʔɛtabʊ 'daŋdaŋ, 10 dantaʔaɡor. Where marked, the stress mark stands at the left edge of the (phonological) word ('nɔʔbɔŋ, 'notɛʔɛtabʊ.., 'daŋ..), except 5 nɔbotaʔ'aɡor where it precedes the final element -aɡor; this is raw wordlist evidence (a handful of forms, one transcriber), not a rule, so no reading…
sources.venue: Numeral Systems of the World's Languages (online database), 'Other Papuan languages' section
